extracted.intended_audience: students, educators, and researchers in journalism and mass communication
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate individual-level influences (education, demographics, values, beliefs, experience, and identity) that shape news selection, framing, and reporting in journalism. Useful for media studies, newsroom policy analysis, and journalism curriculum design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective journalists' actual writing ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Many prospective journalism majors think they can write well but in fact cannot; as a result, many journalism schools have to teach at a more basic level than they prefer, including teaching basic grammar (Stein, 1992b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess incoming students' demonstrated writing skills; curricular expectations should match actual student ability. Anti-pattern: assuming prior competence and omitting basic instruction, which forces remedial teaching and weakens advanced coursework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum orientation: liberal_arts vs technical/skills programs (insider vs outsider)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best approach to mass communication education is debated: some want liberal arts educations with a strong orientation in research, theory, and critical thinking; others want highly technical, skills-oriented programs. Texts are designed either to socialize students to being mass communication 'insiders' or to teach them to look critically at all social institutions (the 'outsiders') (Shoemaker, 1987).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing programs, consider whether the goal is to produce industry-ready practitioners or critically minded analysts. Choice of textbooks and courses will socialize students toward the chosen orientation; faculty orientation typically drives this decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty professional orientation and ongoing engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty reading and professional habits reflect orientation: about 40% keep up with both academic and media industry knowledge, ~30% read only industry publications, ~20% read only scholarly journals, and ~10% keep up with neither (Weaver & Wilhoit, 1986b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty engagement with both scholarly and industry sources shapes curriculum and student perspectives. Evaluate faculty development and incentives to maintain balance between practical skills and theoretical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core competencies of exemplary journalism programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Good journalists must 'know more than a little about a lot of things... must be able to learn quickly. They must write well, and cherish that ability.' Exemplary schools give students the best opportunity to begin mastering these fundamental qualities (Footlick, 1988, p. 69).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess programs on how well they cultivate breadth of knowledge, rapid learning ability, curiosity, and strong writing. Use these competencies as student outcome metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of curricular specialization (sequence organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most departments are organized along media lines (news-editorial, magazine, broadcast, photojournalism, public relations, advertising). Students take few common courses, concentrating on specialized knowledge. Some schools (e.g., Trinity University) have moved to a more general curriculum with common areas: media study/theory, management/research, media writing, and production (Christ & Blanchard, 1988).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether sequence-based specialization or a more integrated curriculum better meets industry needs and educational goals. Consider common-core benefits vs depth in specialized tracks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-driven student choices and supply effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising and public relations sequences are growing fastest; students increasingly reject news-editorial sequences because of 'negative perceptions' like low salaries and lack of creativity (Mann, 1988).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor enrollment trends as indicators of future staffing and talent pipelines for different media sectors; consider interventions (scholarships, showcasing career paths) to rebalance supply for news-editorial roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between liberal arts and professional coursework (accreditor guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Accrediting Council guidelines: ~25% courses inside journalism/mass communication and ~75% in liberal arts and sciences. Some schools want more in-major credit hours to meet modern profession demands (University of Wisconsin withdrew from accrediting system to require more school credits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging program rigor, weigh the tradeoff between broad liberal arts grounding and practical, in-major preparation. Accreditation standards vs institutional aims should be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth in subject-matter expertise vs breadth (double majors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some schools encourage/require double majors (e.g., business + journalism) so graduates have depth in topic areas employers require. Depth (e.g., national security knowledge) can set journalists apart; too few journalists have such specialized knowledge (Burt, 1991).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidate/journalist qualifications on subject expertise for complex beats. Encourage curricular options enabling substantive depth (double majors, minors, specialized tracks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom valuation: tradecraft skills over subject expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors often prefer 'tradecraft' reporting skills over subject-specific expertise; there's a tendency to mistrust specialists as possibly co-opted by their beats, so 'professional distance' can mask ignorance (editor quote: 'If you know how to cover a major fire, you can cover anything').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsroom hiring and assignment norms that privilege versatile reporting skills versus specialist knowledge. Anti-pattern: dismissing expertise and assuming generalists can cover all complex topics equally well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographics and education of journalists as an influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists tend to be better educated and better writers than the average American; backgrounds (family, school, life experiences) shape priorities, expectations, and dreams—and therefore can influence news values and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider demographic and educational composition when analyzing newsroom biases or coverage tendencies. However, organizational routines may moderate these individual-level effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative strength of organizational routines vs individual differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaver and Wilhoit argue that the effect of journalists' demographics on news values/content is probably minor given the importance of organizational routines and constraints (1991).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing content outcomes, evaluate both individual attributes and powerful organizational routines (schedules, beats, editorial policies). Empirical research is needed to isolate these variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender effects on coverage (non-uniform responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies show female magazine publishers gave more favorable coverage to the ERA than male counterparts; female editorialists do not 'respond in lockstep' to women's issues—evaluations occur on an individual basis (Farley, 1978; Goodrick, 1991).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming monolithic coverage based on gender; assess individual editorial judgment and contextual factors. Use empirical studies to detect patterns rather than stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom interpersonal culture changes from increased women presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase of women editors changed newsroom interactions: 'Cheesecake has virtually disappeared. Sexist, off-color jokes are out—totally.' News meetings became less confrontational and more collaborative (Marzolf; Stein, 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how demographic shifts alter workplace norms, meeting styles, and collaboration; these cultural changes can affect story selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment practices and marginalization of minority reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Minority reporters are often assigned minority stories only and then not permitted to write lead stories or direct coverage; assignments may value their ethnicity over journalistic role, leading to undervaluation (example: 1992 LA riots coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess assignment policies for tokenism and unequal access to prominent stories. Anti-pattern: assigning reporters to beats based solely on identity without offering leadership or lead opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity concerns tied to reporter identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors ask whether women should be allowed to cover abortion or whether minorities/gays can cover their own communities objectively; questions imply certain identities might compromise objectivity even though similar questions are not asked of others (e.g., men covering sports/war).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how assumptions about objectivity shape assignment decisions. Consider arguments for transparency about perspective versus strict 'objectivity' norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy vs traditional objectivity debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critique the traditional concept of objectivity, arguing everyone has a point of view and that it is best if the writer's point of view is stated openly; others hold to traditional journalistic objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting editorial norms or evaluating reporting, specify whether the standard is neutral objectivity, transparent subjectivity, or advocacy journalism; document expected disclosures and role boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation improving coverage of community-specific issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Gay and lesbian reporters can 'flag words, phrases or images that mislead or reinforce stereotypes' and their presence can force heterosexual colleagues to confront biases; lack of openly gay reporters harmed AIDS coverage (Randy Shilts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsroom diversity as a determinant of coverage comprehensiveness and sensitivity. Representation is a metric for likely improvements in topic detection and framing for undercovered communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring local/foreign journalists as foreign correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Budget trimming makes it more practical to hire foreign journalists as 'foreign' correspondents rather than sending U.S. reporters abroad; foreign journalists 'should be able to depict foreign reality more accurately than a 'parachuting' foreign correspondent' (Shuster, 1988).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider local hiring for foreign coverage as a quality-improvement and cost-effective strategy. Evaluate reporters' local knowledge, language ability, and cultural competence as part of correspondent selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local community recruitment matters for ethnic coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when Hispanic personnel were recruited, hiring from outside the local community led to failure to identify issues perceived as important by the Hispanic constituency; employment patterns/stereotypes can cause over-emphasis on negative news (Greenberg et al., 1983).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess recruitment strategies for community embeddedness. Favor hiring reporters familiar with local constituencies to improve relevance and reduce stereotyped negative framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of outside career experience (e.g., politics) on credibility and assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists who take jobs in politics may be perceived as 'soiled goods' on return; some editors view government experience positively for covering that beat, others view it negatively for credibility reasons (Ray Jenkins example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate disclosure and reassignment policies for journalists returning from politically aligned roles. Consider how prior employment affects perceived impartiality and beat suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personality type shaping beat preferences and news choices
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 'personality type' in journalism—journalists like excitement and dislike abstractions; this leads them to prefer covering dynamic beats (e.g., Senate vs House, politics vs management) and shapes the kinds of stories produced (Hess, 1981).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing newsroom content, account for personality-driven beat selection and reporter preferences; recruitment and training can diversify temperament mix for broader coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' core values influencing news frames (Gans' list)
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. journalists generally hold 'motherhood' values (favor family, oppose hate) and values associated with the Progressive movement: ethnocentrism, altruistic democracy, responsible capitalism, small‑town pastoralism, individualism, moderatism, social order, and leadership. These values underlie story selection and framing (Gans, 1979).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Gans' value categories to code and analyze news content for recurrent frames (e.g., ethnocentrism or responsible capitalism). Recognize that these values can reflect a mix of conservative and liberal tendencies and may attract value-driven individuals to journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' political orientations and elite vs general differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions of journalists as politically liberal have been widespread; elite journalists (those at prestigious outlets) were found to be more liberal in some studies, while probability samples show journalists overall are only modestly more Democratic than the general population (various surveys summarized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political bias claims, distinguish elite media samples from representative samples; measure party identification and ideological self-placement and analyze how elite clustering may influence high-impact coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom policies on outside partisan/community involvement (conflicts of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many newspapers have policies avoiding active involvement in partisan causes or community affairs that could 'compromise or seem to compromise' fair reporting; relatives' employment or involvement must be disclosed (Washington Post policy). Cases like Sandy Nelson show enforcement can include reassignment or dismissal threats to protect perceived credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional conflict-of-interest policies, disclosure requirements, and enforcement mechanisms. Policies should balance journalists' rights with organizational credibility, with clear definitions of prohibited activities and procedures for recusal or reassignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious affiliation and its effects on religion coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Elite journalists tend to be more secular than journalists as a whole; the religion beat is understaffed and religion is often unevenly or uncritically covered. Analyses show only half of certain religion stories presented skeptical or alternative perspectives (Triplett, 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsroom capacity for religious coverage (number of religion beats/editors), training in religious literacy, and sourcing practices that include skeptical and faith-based perspectives. Undercoverage and uncritical reporting are red flags for inadequate beat expertise or institutional prioritization.
